At the end of Round 5, if total Value meets market demand and cumulative Resource footprints stay below thresholds, all win; otherwise the supply chain collapses under unsustainable stress. Through asymmetric roles, inter-stage negotiation and joint investment, “Upstream Allies” teaches how every link—from farm to fork—must collaborate to achieve true sustainable living.

“Green Legacy” is a cooperative legacy board game for 2–4 players who guide a single family line through six generations on a shared Estate board. Each generation you allocate Action tokens among Farming, Energy, Water, Community and Innovation sites, then draw an Event card (drought, boom‐time, policy shift) that tests your infrastructure. Completed upgrades (solar well, rain garden, permaculture plot, repair workshop) remain for descendants but may decay if neglected. You track three Legacy meters—Environmental Health, Social Well‐Being and Resource Resilience—across generations. At the end of the sixth generation, if all three meters meet the global Sustainability Threshold, your family’s Green Legacy endures and you win. By experiencing how today’s decisions shape tomorrow’s inheritance, players learn long-term planning, trade-offs and intergenerational impacts of sustainable living.

“Flow of Life” is a cooperative tabletop engineering game for 1–4 players who together build a modular marble-run network that models energy, water and waste flows in a community. Each round you draft and place track modules—solar panels (yellow marbles), rain funnels (blue), compost loops (brown)—then release a batch of marbles representing daily resource yields. Marbles routed correctly into reservoirs, batteries or compost bins earn Efficiency Points; marbles lost to spill channels count as pollution. Event cards (drought, heat wave, equipment failure) change marble inputs or disable modules, forcing on-the-fly reconfiguration. Over seven rounds you must reach a shared Sustainability Threshold on the Efficiency meter to win. By designing, testing and adapting a physical resource network in real time, players learn the interdependence of collection, storage, recycling and the costs of waste in sustainable living.

“Common Ground” is a semi-cooperative board game for 3–5 players who each run a household’s sustainability over 12 monthly rounds. On your turn you may:
• Take a personal action (bike commute, plant-based meals, compost setup) to reduce your carbon, water or waste footprint at the cost of time or money tokens.
• Invest in a communal project (solar array, rain garden, tool library) by contributing tokens; completed projects boost the shared Community Meter.
• Trade goods or services (tools, produce, childcare) in the Barter Market to optimize resource flows.

Each round a Monthly Event card (heat wave, subsidy, supply shortage) tests the neighborhood’s resilience. Players track individual Footprint scores while the board displays the Community Meter. If after 12 rounds the Community Meter reaches its target and every player’s Footprint remains below their personal threshold, all win—plus the player with the lowest Footprint is named “Green Neighbor.” By balancing solo choices, shared investments and strategic trading, Common Ground teaches collaboration, circular resource use and the cumulative impact of sustainable living.

“SustainQuest” is a cooperative tabletop role-playing game for 3–6 players who embody community roles (Water Engineer, Forest Keeper, Solar Technician, Educator, Farmer, Artisan). Over eight “Years,” the group holds narrative scenes in which they spend limited Action Points on projects—rainwater harvesting, reforestation, solar microgrids, permaculture gardens, public workshops—and then draw an Event Card (drought, pest outbreak, funding cuts, grant opportunities) that tests their four Resource Tracks (Water, Energy, Biodiversity, Social Cohesion). When a track falls to zero, a Crisis token is placed; accumulating three Crises ends the campaign in collapse. If the players survive all eight Years without three Crises, they win, having collaboratively forged a living story of resilience and balanced ecological, social and economic needs.

Greenwash is a 6–10-player social-deduction and policymaking card game where players secretly take on roles as Environmental Advocates or Greenwashers (industry insiders). Each round:
1. Draw Initiative cards (e.g. “Community Solar,” “Eco-Label Campaign,” “Carbon Capture R&D”).
2. In secret, Greenwashers pick high-footprint cards disguised as green. Advocates pick genuine low-impact Initiatives.
3. All discuss and vote to enact one Initiative; enacted policies adjust shared Meters for Carbon, Funding and Public Trust.
4. Vote to expose a suspected Greenwasher—if correct they’re removed; if wrong the Carbon Meter spikes.
Victory: Advocates win by passing four genuine Initiatives or exposing all Greenwashers. Greenwashers win by maxing the Carbon Meter or outnumbering Advocates. Through bluffing, debate and real-world impact tracking, Greenwash teaches players to spot greenwashing, weigh policy trade-offs and understand how hidden agendas can undermine sustainable living.

“Biomimicry Builders” is a cooperative tile-placement game for 2–4 players who design a “Living City” by laying hex tiles inspired by nature’s solutions—termite-mound ventilation, lotus-leaf water repellent, honeycomb structural grids, mycelium waste-recycling networks. Each tile grants efficiency bonuses in energy, water or materials. On each turn you draw a Stress card (heat wave, drought, resource shortage) that forces the group to spend or reconfigure your city’s tiles to buffer impacts. You may instead invest Action points to research a new biomimetic upgrade—when built, it permanently boosts one resource system. Over six rounds your goal is to keep all three resource meters within safe bands; if you succeed, your Living City thrives. Through patterning natural strategies into your layout and balancing immediate stress with long-term research, players learn how biomimicry drives sustainable living.

EcoGrid is a 1–6 player roll-and-write game where everyone co-creates a sustainable region on personal grid sheets. Each round you roll Resource dice (Sun, Rain, Biomass, Materials) and a Climate die (Drought, Storm, Heatwave, Incentive). Players draft Resource dice to mark actions—installing solar farms, planting permaculture guilds, routing rainwater channels or building repair hubs—onto their grids, scoring synergy bonuses for adjacency and closed loops. Unpicked dice feed the communal “Green Index” meter. After 12 rounds, if the Green Index meets its target and individual Sustainability Goals are reached, all players win. EcoGrid teaches resource allocation, system interdependence and trade-offs in sustainable living.

“EcoPress” is a semi-cooperative board game for 3–5 players who take turns as editors of a small town’s newspaper. Each round represents one edition:

• Draft Story cards (e.g. “Community Garden Launch,” “Local Factory Pollution,” “Bike-to-Work Day”) and Ad cards (e.g. “Fast-Fashion Sale,” “Organic Co-op Promo”).  
• Negotiate which headlines make the front page. Stories and ads adjust three shared meters—Sustainability, Public Trust and Revenue—up or down.  
• Draw an Event card (heat wave, subsidy cut, grassroots campaign) to see how your previous coverage alters real-world outcomes: crops flourish, protests erupt or ad income shifts.

At the end of six editions, if your Sustainability meter is above the target while Trust and Revenue remain healthy, you save the paper—and your town thrives; if any meter collapses, the paper folds and the community suffers. Through balancing truthful reporting, funding pressures and public engagement, EcoPress teaches how media choices shape environmental awareness, economic viability and collective action in sustainable living.

“Pollination Pioneers” is a cooperative worker‐placement board game for 2–5 players who restore regional pollinator health over eight seasons. Each turn players assign Worker tokens to four action areas: Flower Planting (gather Nectar tokens), Habitat Building (earn Shelter tokens), Policy Advocacy (generate Funding tokens) and Public Outreach (draw Education cards). Event cards—drought, invasive species, pesticide spill—trigger stress checks against a shared Pollinator Health track. Players spend Resource tokens to buffer events or upgrade action areas with modules (seed banks, wildflower corridors, pesticide filters). At each season’s end, leftover tokens convert to Pollinator Health points; if the health meter reaches its threshold before eight rounds expire, all win. By balancing agriculture, habitat, policy and education, players learn how integrated efforts sustain pollinators and the crop systems they support.

GreenPrint Studio is a competitive tile‐draft and floor‐plan board game for 2–4 players who act as eco‐architects designing a tiny home. Each round:
• Draft Material cards (bamboo flooring, recycled steel, straw bales) with embodied carbon, insulation R‐values and cost.  
• Place Room tiles (kitchen, living, bathroom, rooftop garden) onto your 5×5 grid blueprint, orienting windows and overhangs to maximize passive solar gain or shading.  
• Install Fixture tokens (rainwater tank, solar panels, composting loo) by spending Resource cubes (money, labor, permits).  
After five design phases you assess your Home’s Sustainability Score—energy demand, water efficiency and footprint reduction—with bonuses for circular-economy upgrades (autoclaved straw panels, greywater loop). The highest combined score of comfort and low impact wins, teaching material trade-offs, passive design principles and lifecycle thinking in sustainable living.

“Swap ’n’ Sustain” is a semi-cooperative card game for 2–5 players who each manage a “Wish Board” of sustainable home upgrades (e-bike, rain barrel, compost bin, solar lantern). Every round players draw Resource dice (wood, metal, fabric, electronics) and repair Skill cards, then craft Upgrades by spending matching resources. After crafting they enter a Swap Phase: trading partially repaired items, scrap or Skill cards to help others finish theirs. At the end of each round an Event card (e-waste audit, freecycle fair, tool-share launch, repair café) awards Community Points for waste diverted or shared services used. After ten rounds, if the group reaches its Community Point target and the shared Landfill meter stays below its limit, all win—having learned how repair, reuse, sharing and community exchange build a circular, sustainable lifestyle.

EcoDomino: Chain Reaction is a cooperative tile-placement game for 2–6 players who build a contiguous network of sustainable actions. Each player holds domino-style Action Tiles printed with an “input” icon (rainwater, organics, sun, foot-power) and an “output” icon (filtered water, compost, electricity, transport). On your turn you place a tile so its input matches an adjacent tile’s output, creating chains that model real resource flows (e.g. rain→filter→irrigation). At the end of each round, a Demand Card reveals community needs (liters of water, kWh, meal servings, clean journeys) which you fulfill by counting chains that reach corresponding “service hubs.” Event Cards (drought, blackout, festival, subsidy) then modify available tiles or shift demands. After six Demand rounds, if your network met all targets without orphan tiles, you win—learning how local actions interconnect into sustainable systems and why planning flows prevents resource dead-ends.

“EcoFestival” is a cooperative board game for 2–6 players who act as planning committees for a week-long music festival. Each player oversees one department—Energy, Waste, Food & Drink, Transport or Experience—and in four phases (Planning, Setup, Live Event, Wrap-Up) allocates limited Budget and Resource tokens to sustainable options: solar generators, composting toilets, plant-based vendors, shuttle services, reusable merch. Phase Event cards (rainstorm, crowd surge, vendor strike) force interdepartmental coordination to balance three Impact meters—Carbon, Waste, Satisfaction. Bonus Innovation tokens reward green upgrades like bike valet or zero-waste stages. If all meters stay within targets by Wrap-Up, the festival ‘wins,’ teaching real-world trade-offs and collaboration in sustainable living.

“Carbon Compass” is a cooperative board game for 1–4 players who plan daily travel in a growing city. Over eight “days,” players place Transport cards—Walk, Bike, Bus or EV—onto a modular map to connect Home, Work, School and Market. Each mode has time, cost and carbon, water or waste footprints. At day’s end an Event card (Rush-Hour Jam, Fare Subsidy, Heatwave) alters travel or footprint values. Players spend earned Community Tokens to build city upgrades (bike lanes, solar bus stops, rain gardens) that permanently reduce future footprints or travel time. After eight days, if the group’s cumulative footprint stays below the shared sustainability threshold, the city thrives and all win. Carbon Compass teaches time–resource trade-offs, how green infrastructure compounds benefits and the cumulative impact of everyday transport choices.

Code Green is a cooperative programming board game for 1–4 players who sequence eco-drones on a modular city grid to clean pollution, plant trees and recharge at solar stations before power runs out. Each round players draft Command cards (Move, Scan, Recycle, Plant, Charge) to build a shared instruction queue; then all drones execute their programs simultaneously, clearing pollution tokens and sowing saplings. Climate Event cards (heatwave, flood, policy rebate) alter the board or grant bonus solar energy. If players achieve a target “Green Coverage” rating within eight cycles, the city thrives. By planning, debugging and managing battery life and resources, Code Green teaches systems thinking, efficiency trade-offs and the impact of coordinated actions in sustainable living.

“Green Rituals” is a semi-cooperative board game for 1–4 players who cultivate daily sustainable habits over a 21-day cycle. Each player has a personal “Day Planner” board with three slots (Morning, Afternoon, Evening). At the start of each day, players draft Habit cards (e.g. Meatless Meal, Bike Commute, DIY Cleaning) and assign them to slots by spending limited Willpower tokens. Completing a habit earns Impact Points and removes Footprint tokens; failing one costs Willpower. Every 7 days an Event card (e.g. heat wave, work crunch, subsidy) forces a group Challenge—players must contribute Impact Points or spend shared Resource tokens to avoid setbacks (extra Footprint, lost Willpower). After 21 days, if the group’s total Impact exceeds the Sustainability Threshold, all players “unlock” a Community Bonus; the individual with the longest habit streak wins the title “Master Ritualist.” Through slot-planning, resource trade-offs and periodic crises, Green Rituals teaches how small, consistent daily actions accumulate into lasting sustainable living and how social support helps overcome real-life challenges.

“Garden Grid” is a competitive card‐draft and grid‐placement game for 2–4 players who each build a 3×3 permaculture garden. On your turn you draft Plant cards (nitrogen-fixers, pollinator-attractors, ground-covers) or Technique cards (compost, mulch, drip irrigation), then place one into your grid to activate adjacency bonuses (e.g. a bee-flower next to fruit yields extra harvest). After each of three “Seasons,” you resolve a Weather Event (drought, blossom boom, pest outbreak) that tests your water, pollination and soil metrics, modified by your installed Techniques. Gardens earn Food tokens and Ecosystem Balance points; if you meet your harvest goal while keeping Balance above zero, you win. Through drafting, spatial planning and event adaptation, Garden Grid teaches players the principles of species synergy, resource cycling and resilient food systems in sustainable living.

“Zero Waste Kitchen” is a 2–4-player cooperative card-and-tile game simulating one month in a shared household kitchen. Each “week” you draw random Ingredient tiles (produce, grains, dairy, scraps) into a communal Fridge, then draft and play Recipe cards that consume ingredients and generate Leftover tiles. In a Cleanup phase you assign Leftovers to Compost or Landfill—Compost tiles become Compost tokens that can be spent to “grow” new ingredients, while Landfill tiles incur Sustainability penalties. Each round a Week-end Event card (power outage, farmers’ market sale, spoilage) forces menu adjustments or bonus yields. After four weeks you total your Nutrition Score (from meals) minus Landfill penalties and check Compost rate; if nutrition meets dietary goals and ≥80 % of scraps were composted, all players win. Players learn menu planning, seasonal sourcing, batch cooking, preservation and composting to turn waste into resources.

Green Bid is a semi-cooperative auction game for 3–6 players acting as municipal planners racing to fund sustainable projects before a global Crisis meter fills. Each round three Project cards (e.g. solar farm, rainwater harvesters, bike network) lie face-up with carbon, water and cost values. Players secretly bid Budget tokens to win projects—highest bid installs the project and immediately reduces the shared Footprint meter; losers recover half their bid. After each auction an Event card (heat wave, drought, green subsidy) shifts the Crisis meter or grants bonus Budget to the lowest bidder. Over eight auctions, if the Crisis meter hasn’t maxed out and the Footprint meter has hit its reduction target, all win—teaching trade-offs in public investment, auction dynamics, and the impact of prioritizing green infrastructure.

“Waste Warriors” is a cooperative dexterity board game for 2–5 players who take turns flicking colored “waste” tokens (paper, plastic, metal, food, e-waste) into matching bins on a modular board before time runs out. Each bin has a weekly capacity; overflow generates Pollution Points. After each round, players use accumulated Pollution to fund upgrades—mobile recycling units, community composters, repair cafés—that expand capacities or auto-process certain wastes. Random Event cards (storms, power outages, subsidies) introduce new constraints or bonuses. After four rounds (weeks), if total Pollution stays below the critical threshold, the community thrives and all players win—teaching accurate sorting, infrastructure investment and the real-time consequences of waste overflow in sustainable living.

“Evolution Exodus” is a cooperative card-and-board game for 2–5 players who guide a species through five Climate Epochs. At each turn players draft Trait cards (e.g. drought tolerance, heat shock proteins, migration instinct, symbiosis) into a shared Genome tableau, then allocate limited Energy tokens to express those traits in individual Population markers. An Environment card each Epoch (glacial freeze, monsoon, wildfire, sea-level rise) rearranges Biome tiles on the modular map, imposing challenge thresholds. After allocation, players test Survival: compare Trait strengths against Biome demands; failures cost Population and Biodiversity points. Between Epochs they may sacrifice short-term reproduction for genetic diversity boosts. If, after the final Epoch, they retain at least 30 Population and 15 Biodiversity points, the species endures. Through drafting, adaptive trade-offs and managing genetic diversity in a changing world, players learn how evolution fosters resilience and why sustainable ecosystems depend on biological variety.

“SustainSupply Sprint” is a semi-cooperative racing board game for 2–6 players who each pilot a token around a circular “Life Cycle” track with zones: Extraction, Energy, Manufacturing, Retail, Consumption, Disposal and Recycling. On your turn you roll a die and choose either the Fast Track (shorter but adds Carbon tokens) or the Green Route (longer but grants Impact tokens). Landing on Event spaces triggers Scenario cards (oil shortage, recycling breakthrough, subsidy) that force trade-offs—spend Impact to offset Carbon or suffer Crisis penalties. Accumulated Carbon tokens fill a global Crisis meter; if it maxes out, all players pause to resolve a Recycling mini-puzzle (sorting resource tiles) to reduce Carbon. The first player to complete three full laps with their personal Carbon under a threshold and the Crisis meter under its limit wins. Through route choices, resource management and collaborative crisis response, players learn how balancing convenience against sustainable options shapes individual footprints and community resilience.

“Carbon Countdown” is a competitive estimation party game for 3–8 players. Each round an Item card (e.g. “1 kg beef,” “200 km flight,” “latte”) is revealed and everyone secretly writes their guess of its carbon footprint in kg CO₂e. Guesses closest without exceeding the true value (printed on the back) score Carbon Points equal to that value; overshooters score zero. Exact matches earn Upgrade Credits, which can be spent mid-game to buy Upgrade cards (e-bike, solar roof, plant-based diet) that deduct fixed Carbon Points from a player’s final total. After 10 rounds, players subtract deductions from their Carbon Points—the lowest total wins. By repeatedly estimating real-world footprints and investing in sustainable upgrades, players learn how everyday choices add up and how lifestyle changes compound to shrink their personal carbon footprint.

Eco Sleuth is a cooperative deduction board game for 2–5 players who investigate and solve environmental crises in a small town. A modular board shows Water, Air and Land zones, each afflicted by hidden Pollution cards (chemical runoff, smog, landfill overflow). Players move their Investigator tokens to gather Clue cards—sampling soil, interviewing residents, inspecting factories—then share intel to deduce each zone’s primary Pollution source and choose a matching Solution card (wetland restoration, emissions scrubbers, zero‐waste ordinance). Correct matches reduce the Crisis meter; wrong ones advance it. Between cases, players spend earned Community Influence tokens to unlock green infrastructure upgrades that grant bonus clues or allow re‐draws. If all zones are cleared before the Crisis meter maxes out, the town is saved. Through gathering evidence, diagnosing root causes and applying targeted sustainable remedies under time pressure, Eco Sleuth teaches systems thinking, the interplay of personal choices and policy, and the steps needed for resilient, sustainable living.

EcoMatch is a cooperative match-3 mobile game where players swap resource icons (water drops, solar rays, compost piles, bike wheels) to trigger real-world sustainable actions—irrigating crops, powering homes with renewables, composting waste and expanding bike lanes. Each match fills meters that unlock community projects and educational tips, while periodic Crisis events (drought, blackout, landfill overflow) force players to focus specific icons to restore balance. Over ten chapters the team transforms a polluted town into a resilient green hub, learning how small, everyday choices compound into lasting sustainable living habits.

Thread for Tomorrow is a cooperative tabletop weaving game for 2–4 players who physically “weave” resource flows on a magnetic loom board. The board’s warp lines are printed with node symbols for Water (blue), Energy (yellow), Food (green) and Waste (brown). Each round:
1. Draw a Demand card specifying one or more network loops to complete (e.g. connect two Water nodes to one Food node).
2. Draft Resource Thread tiles of matching colors and weave them along the loom’s magnetic grid to close loops.
3. Resolve a Crisis card (drought, blackout, spoilage, overflow) that may cut or shift existing threads, forcing on-the-fly repairs.

Closed loops earn Sustainability Points; broken loops incur Penalty Tokens. After eight rounds, if players have met or exceeded the shared Sustainability Target without running out of Repair Tokens, they “finish” the tapestry—an interwoven map of their resilient community—and win. Thread for Tomorrow teaches systems thinking, the interdependence of resource networks and the importance of repair and balance in sustainable living.

Photon Pathways is a cooperative board-puzzle game for 1–4 players who act as eco-engineers designing a village’s solar network. Over eight rounds (time slots) a Sun track sets the sun’s angle and a Weather card sets light intensity. Players take turns placing Mirror, Lens and Solar Panel tiles on a shared hex grid to reflect and refract a single incoming beam into target Building tokens (homes, water heaters, greenhouses) that require electric, thermal or daylight energy. Surplus light can be routed into Battery modules for storage; misdirected rays spill into Waste channels, raising Loss markers. After eight slots, if delivered energy meets each building’s demand under variable angles and weather, all players win. By solving spatial ray-tracing puzzles under changing conditions, Photon Pathways teaches solar capture, energy storage, distribution and the challenges of renewable variability in sustainable living.

Greenify is a cooperative mobile app that turns real-world eco-habits into a shared mission. Each day players receive three randomized “Eco Missions” (e.g. plant-based meal, 5-minute shower, upcycle project, public-transit commute). Completing a mission in real life and uploading a photo or geotag earns Green Points and fills the group’s “Carbon Savings Meter,” while missed missions trigger optional mini-challenges to recover. Weekly “Crisis Events” (heatwave, water shortage) demand specific mission types to defend the shared meter. If, after a month, the Carbon Savings Meter exceeds its target, players unlock advanced mission tiers (home energy audit, community garden build) and concise educational modules. By gamifying daily sustainable actions, feedback and cooperative milestones, Greenify teaches how consistent small choices compound into community-wide impact.

ChronoGreen is a cooperative legacy board game for 2–4 players acting as Time Agents who repair Earth’s timeline through four eras—Industrial Age, Tech Boom, Climate Crisis and Sustainable Future. Each era uses its own board, resources and Challenge cards (factory spills, Gold Rush deforestation, hurricanes, resource wars). Players spend Action Points to introduce innovations (smokestack scrubbers, solar grids, circular-economy policies, regenerative cities), place Legacy Markers that permanently alter later eras, and manage a Paradox Meter—too many failed challenges fractures the timeline and ends the game. If you complete all eras with the Ecological Stability Meter above the threshold, you win. ChronoGreen teaches how past choices echo through history, the urgency of timely interventions and the interconnected nature of sustainable living.

“Forest Stewards” is a cooperative board game for 1–4 players who manage a shared forest ecosystem across five seasons. Each turn, players spend limited Time Tokens on actions: Selective Harvest (gain Wood), Replant Saplings (restore tree cover), Wildlife Support (increase Biodiversity), Watershed Care (boost Water Quality), or Eco-Tourism (earn Revenue). Wood and Revenue are spent to build Eco-Infrastructure cards (e.g. Rain Gardens, Wildlife Corridors) that permanently improve one metric. At the end of each season a Disturbance card (wildfire, storm, disease, drought) tests tree density, biodiversity, water health and community support and may inflict damage if thresholds aren’t met. After five seasons, if all four metrics reach sustainability targets, all players win. Forest Stewards teaches balancing resource use with ecosystem health, long-term planning and the interdependence of forestry, biodiversity, water and community in sustainable living.

EcoStep Village is a cooperative mobile game for 1–6 players that turns real-world movement into digital village building to teach sustainable living. Each player syncs a step‐counter or bike ride tracker to earn three resource tokens—Energy (kWh), Water (liters) and Waste Credits—based on distance and activity type (walking, cycling, gardening). Players merge tokens to construct and upgrade village modules (solar microgrid, rainwater harvesters, compost centers, bike-share hubs) on a shared map. Periodic Climate Events (heatwave, drought, waste surge) force teams to spend stored resources or suffer meter penalties. Completing green upgrades unlocks permanent buffs—lower resource costs, bonus Citizen Happiness—and unlocks short, science-backed lifestyle tips. The goal is to raise the village’s Sustainability Index to 100% before each seasonal deadline. By linking daily eco-actions to in-game infrastructure, EcoStep Village teaches how consistent, collective habits reduce footprints and build resilient communities.

Sprout Society is a hybrid board-and-garden game for 2–4 players. Over six “Growing Weeks,” each player tends a real microgreen tray at home while playing on a shared board. Each round you draw Care cards (Water, Nutrients, Shade, Pest Control) and assign Action tokens; successful in-game care earns Growth Tokens to apply in real life (extra mist, shade cloth, organic spray). Weekly Weather cards (drought, overcast, heat) force strategic adjustments both on board and at home. At the end, players weigh their harvests to meet the board’s “Community Kitchen” target and earn bonus points for tray health. By tying every decision to living plants, Sprout Society teaches resource stewardship, the ripple effects of care choices and the rewards of sustainable gardening.

EcoExchange is a competitive stock-market simulation for 3–6 players who invest in five fictional companies—FossilCo, AgroChem, RenewCorp, RecycleWorks and WaterSmart—each rated by Profit and Sustainability indices. On each of eight rounds players:

1. Trading Phase: buy or sell shares at current prices.  
2. R&D Phase: spend cash to play Project cards that raise a company’s Sustainability index (at the cost of Profit points) or boost Profit (at the cost of Sustainability).  
3. Event Phase: draw a Market Event (carbon tax, oil spill, green subsidy, activist campaign, extreme weather) that shifts share prices according to each company’s Profit×Sustainability profile.

At game end players liquidate portfolios; final score = cash + share value + a bonus for average Sustainability across holdings. The highest total wins. By weighing short-term gains against long-term green investments and reacting to market events, players learn how capital flows shape corporate behavior and the real-world trade-offs of sustainable living.

Green Story Weavers is a cooperative storytelling card game for 2–6 players. Each turn you play one Story card—Character, Setting, Action or Crisis—to build a shared narrative of a town. Action cards depict sustainable practices (community garden, bike-share, rainwater harvest) that raise three dials on the Storyboard—Ecology, Economy and Well-Being—while Crisis cards (heat wave, pollution spill, budget cut) deplete them. If any dial hits zero the plot darkens and recovery costs extra turns. After eight chapters, if all dials stay above the victory line, players win, having woven a living tale of how everyday green choices build resilient futures.

HomeGrid is a cooperative board game for 1–4 players who manage a smart home’s 24-hour schedule to minimize energy and water footprints. The board shows a timeline with Energy and Water meters. Each turn you draw Occupant Demand cards (e.g. Shower, Laundry, Cooking, Irrigation) and assign Appliance cards (Solar Heater, Rainwater Toilet, Heat-pump Dryer) into hour slots. Weather Event cards adjust solar output or rainfall catchment. Appliances scheduled during high-generation slots cost no resources; off-peak use draws from the grid or well and adds Footprint tokens. If all demands are met and both meters stay under their thresholds by day’s end, you win—learning how demand management, smart devices and syncing usage with renewables drive sustainable living.

“HeatShare” is a cooperative tile‐placement board game for 2–5 players who together build and manage a shared district‐heating network through a harsh winter. The modular board is a grid of House tiles (each with a daily heat‐demand rating) surrounding a Central Plant. Each turn:
1. Draw a Temperature card (–10 °C to +5 °C) that multiplies each house’s demand.
2. Spend Action points to place Network tiles (pipes, heat pumps, solar‐thermal collectors), play Insulation cards on houses or install Heat‐Storage modules.
3. Allocate Fuel tokens (biomass, geothermal, solar‐heat) to meet total demand. Any unmet demand adds Cold‐Markers; excess fuel generates Emission points.
After ten “days,” if no House has three Cold‐Markers and total Emissions stay below the threshold, the network survives the winter. HeatShare teaches insulation’s impact, load balancing, renewable integration and collective investment in efficient, low‐carbon heating.

“EcoBalance” is a cooperative board game for 2–5 players built around a physical see-saw platform. Each round, players draw Project cards (e.g. solar array, rain garden, repair café), each with weight values and resource effects. On their turn, a player places or removes resource cubes (energy, water, waste) on the see-saw to simulate balancing environmental inputs and outputs, then may install the corresponding Project tile to earn Sustainability Points. Event cards (heat wave, drought, subsidy) force players to add “Pressure Cubes” or shift existing weights, testing the group’s ability to rebalance. If the board tips beyond ±10° three times, the community suffers a setback; if they reach the shared Sustainability Target first, they win—learning that sustainable living requires constant trade-offs, equilibrium and coordinated action.

“EcoSound: Sustainable Symphony” is a cooperative rhythm board-and-app game for 2–4 players who play Resource Action cards in time to an app-generated beat, amplifying their effects when perfectly synchronized. The board tracks four meters—Energy, Water, Waste, Community—and each card (e.g. “Install Solar Array,” “Harvest Rainwater,” “Set Up Compost,” “Host Repair Café”) moves meters up or down. At random intervals the app signals a “Crisis Drop” (heatwave, drought, waste surge) during which players must play matching cards together in rhythm to stabilize all meters. Perfectly timed sequences earn Harmony Tokens that unlock lasting green upgrades on the board. If, by the end of the final song, all four meters remain within safe bands, the players complete the Sustainable Symphony—having learned that well-timed, coordinated actions across sectors compose a resilient, balanced system.

EcoKitchen: Zero-Waste Rush is a real-time cooperative video game for 2–4 players who run an eco-restaurant. Each level you race to prepare plant-based menus, harvest from your on-site garden and divert scraps into compost, broth or upcycled dishes using limited water, energy and ingredients. You must coordinate chopping, cooking and cleaning stations to minimize waste, while random events (power outages, spoilage, equipment breakdowns) force instant adaptation. Earned Sustainability Stars let you install green upgrades—solar stovetops, greywater recyclers, regenerative gardens—that permanently cut resource use. Survive successive dinner shifts to build a net-zero-waste eatery, learning menu planning, circular-kitchen practices and the real-time trade-offs of sustainable living.

Skyline Synergy is a cooperative board game for 2–5 players who manage sustainability in a multi-story apartment building. Each round players draw Lifestyle cards (diet, commute, comfort needs) and Building Event cards (energy shortages, subsidies, ordinances), then spend limited Action tokens and resource cubes (Energy, Water, Waste) to install in-unit upgrades (green walls, efficient appliances, compost bins) or invest in shared modules (solar façade, greywater loop, rooftop garden). A central tile-laying “network module” board requires players to physically link pipes and wiring across floors to activate building-wide bonuses. After 12 rounds, if the network loops are complete and the collective Footprint stays below the target, all win—learning how individual choices and cooperative infrastructure build resilient, sustainable communities.

“Second Life” is a semi‐cooperative board game for 2–5 players managing product lifecycles in a shared community. Each turn a player draws an Item card (appliance, garment, gadget) with a Durability track and Material Value. They roll a Usage die to degrade durability, then draw an Event card (repair opportunity, obsolescence, donation request). The player chooses one action:
• Repair: spend Resource tokens to restore Durability and earn Utility points.
• Donate: pass the item to another player for half its remaining Utility.
• Upcycle: convert the item into Material tokens for Community Upgrades.
• Recycle: break the item into raw Material tokens immediately.

An item can change hands up to three times before it must be Upcycled or Recycled. Material tokens fund shared Community Upgrades (repair workshop, material bank), granting group bonuses. When the Item deck is exhausted, players total their Product Utility points (uses × points) minus Waste penalties; if group Waste stays below a target, all win. The highest individual Utility score earns the title “Master Recycler.” Second Life teaches circular economy principles—repair, reuse, donation and material recovery—and the trade‐offs in end‐of‐life decisions for sustainable living.

“Neighbor Nexus” is a semi-cooperative board game for 2–6 players. Each player manages a household board tracking Energy, Water and Waste budgets and holds a secret Lifestyle Profile (e.g. Family of Four, Senior Living Alone, Remote Worker) with unique goals and constraints. Each round (one week) consists of:
1. Planning Phase: play Action cards (Bike Commute, Greywater Retrofit, Bulk-Buy Co-op) to adjust personal metrics.
2. Community Phase: pool tokens on the Neighborhood board to build shared Projects (solar co-op, rain garden, repair café) that unlock global buffs.
3. Crisis Check: draw a Crisis card (heat wave, supply shortage, policy change) that tests both personal and community metrics; shortfalls add Footprint markers.

After eight weeks, if the Neighborhood sustainability score stays above its threshold and no individual exceeds their personal footprint limit, all win—learning how tailored household decisions and collective infrastructure investments combine to create truly sustainable living.

CycleCity is a hybrid fitness-and-strategy game for 2–6 players in which real-world pedaling on stationary bikes (or via a cycling app) generates “Energy,” “Water” and “Momentum” tokens used to build a shared digital eco-city. Each day:
• Players pedal to earn tokens.
• Tokens fund sustainable zones—solar farms, rain gardens, bike lanes, transit hubs—whose adjacency grants synergy bonuses.
• Random Demand Events (heatwaves, festivals, rush hours) force reallocation of tokens to stabilize power, cooling and transport networks.
Over a seven-day campaign, players must meet daily pedaling goals while keeping city metrics (emissions, water use, transit efficiency) within safe thresholds. Success yields carbon neutrality and unlocks advanced scenarios (microgrids, circular water loops), teaching how personal effort, renewable generation and urban planning interconnect in sustainable living.

“Shared Seas” is a semi-cooperative board game for 2–4 players who each represent a coastal nation managing ocean health and fisheries. A central Ocean board tracks Fish Population, Pollution and Temperature. Each “Year” players secretly allocate Action cubes to Fishing, Cleanup, Marine Reserves or Green-Fuel Shipping. After allocations resolve, players draw Climate cards (heatwave, oil spill, ocean acidification) that modify ocean metrics. If Fish Population or Water Quality ever collapse, all lose; if they survive ten years, players score Sustainability (healthy ocean metrics) plus Revenue (fish harvested) and Cooperation (shared investments). The highest combined score wins. By balancing personal gain against shared stewardship and responding to real-time crises, players learn the interconnected challenges and trade-offs of sustainable living on a global scale.

Carbon Cartographers is a cooperative map-drawing and resource-management game for 2–6 players. Beginning with a blank regional grid, players take turns sketching Transport Corridors (road, rail, pipeline) that each cost carbon, water and material tokens. On your turn you may:
• Draw a new corridor segment, consuming resource tokens and adding Pollution markers.
• Play an Upgrade card (Electrify Rail, Biogas Retrofit, Carbon Capture Node) to convert existing lines into low-impact routes.
• Redeploy Resource tokens to repair or reroute damaged segments.

After each round a Climate Event card (flood, heatwave, material shortage) strikes specific grid sectors, destroying unprotected corridors and forcing players to adapt. Players share a global Sustainability Meter that rises when upgrades outnumber new polluting builds and falls when damage exceeds repairs. If they meet the target Meter before the Resource deck depletes, they win—learning infrastructure planning trade-offs, retrofit benefits over new construction, and how regional resource flows interconnect in sustainable living.

“Pantry Patrol” is a semi-cooperative board-and-app game for 2–5 players who each manage a household’s weekly grocery shopping. Each round players draw Meal Plan cards (recipes and nutrition targets), then draft or scan Product cards (produce, grains, proteins, packaged goods)—each tagged with real-world carbon, water and packaging scores via the companion app. After “shopping,” they allocate ingredients to meals and resolve Food Waste: unused or expired items become Waste cubes unless traded or composted at the Community Pantry. Event cards (seasonal shortages, packaging bans, farmers’ market sales) force menu pivots or bonus app challenges to source local producers. Players earn Sustainability Points for meeting nutrition goals with low footprints and minimal waste; if the group hits its monthly Sustainability Target before the deck runs out, all win. Pantry Patrol teaches strategic meal planning, the environmental cost of food choices, packaging trade-offs and the power of communal sharing in sustainable living.

“SolarChef” is a cooperative board game for 1–4 players who must feed a village using only solar energy over a seven-day cooking festival. The game board shows a circular “Sun Dial” track (hours 6 AM–6 PM) and weather deck (sunny, partly cloudy, overcast). Each player starts with one solar-oven token, a water tank, drying rack and three random Recipe cards (e.g. soup, steamed vegetables, dried fruit)—each requiring specific “sun-hours,” water heating or dehydration steps.

On each hour turn:
• Reveal the next weather card—clouds reduce available solar energy cubes.  
• Players spend energy cubes to place ovens on recipes, heat water or dehydrate ingredients.  
• Any unused solar energy can be banked in thermal batteries for nighttime water purification.

At dusk, resolve all recipes: completed dishes earn Nutrition points and refill shared Water reserves; under-cooked or spoiled recipes generate Waste tokens. Replenish ingredients and advance to the next day. After seven days, if the group has met or exceeded the village’s cumulative Nutrition target and kept Waste under the spoilage threshold, everyone wins. SolarChef teaches the importance of renewable variability, energy storage, water reuse and meal planning in sustainable living.

“Trail Guardians” is a cooperative board game for 2–5 players who act as park stewards designing and maintaining a national park’s trail network while protecting its ecosystem. Each round (one month) players spend Action points to:
• Lay or upgrade Trail tiles (gravel paths, boardwalks, switchbacks) that open new Visitor routes but add Erosion tokens.
• Deploy Eco-measures (check dams, native plantings, composting toilets, solar shuttle stops) to reduce erosion, waste and carbon footprints.
• Run Education Programs (guided hikes, wildlife talks) to earn Community Support tokens that buffer against crises.
Visitors appear each round as meeples that travel your trails—if their path intersects damage or lacks signage they generate Waste and Stress markers.

At month’s end you draw an Event card (flash flood, wildfire risk, invasive species outbreak, park funding boost) that tests your four Metrics—Biodiversity, Soil Health, Visitor Satisfaction and Carbon Emissions. Deficits force players to spend resources or accept Penalty tokens. After twelve rounds, if all Metrics meet sustainability targets, the park thrives and the players win—having learned how trail planning, visitor management and habitat restoration must balance to achieve sustainable living in protected landscapes.

Aquifer Quest is a cooperative board game for 2–4 players who manage a shared groundwater basin through four seasons. A modular hex grid represents recharge zones, farms, industry and urban districts—each tile generates water inflows or pollution risks. Each round players draft and play Action cards (Build Recharge Pond, Plant Riparian Buffer, Upgrade Treatment Plant, Regulate Pumping) and assign limited Engineer tokens to execute them. At season’s end a Climate Event card (drought, heavy rains, chemical spill) adds or removes Water and Contaminant tokens on tiles. If after four seasons the total Water tokens remain within reservoir capacity and Contaminant tokens stay below safety thresholds, the basin is sustainable and all win—teaching how land use, recharge and remediation balance to protect clean groundwater.

Mycelial Matrix is a cooperative board game for 2–6 players who simulate a fungal resource network across a hex‐tile landscape of Energy, Water, Food, Waste and Community nodes. Each round you draw an Event card (drought, oil spill, heat wave, subsidy), then spend Action tokens to place colored beads (resources) at supply nodes and physically string matching‐color yarn from supply to demand hubs, routing beads along the threads. Successfully delivered beads satisfy hub demands and advance the shared Sustainability tracker. Misrouted beads, broken threads or running out of yarn add Stress tokens; three Stress cause Network Collapse and a loss. After ten rounds, if all hub demands are met and the network holds, players win—learning how interconnected, efficient “mycelial” networks underpin resilient, sustainable systems.

Greenlight City is a cooperative board game for 2–5 players who manage traffic flow in a growing metropolis. On a modular grid of streets, each turn cars enter at the edges and line up at intersections. Players take turns switching individual traffic lights (North–South vs. East–West) or investing shared tokens to build bike lanes, bus stops or smart‐signal upgrades. After each switch, vehicles advance and idling cars generate Emission cubes. At the end of each round an Event card (rush hour surge, roadworks, heat wave) adds extra cars or blocks lanes. After ten rounds, if total Emissions stay under the city’s threshold and average travel time remains below the target, all win. By balancing green infrastructure investments with real‐time signal timing, Greenlight City teaches how coordinated planning and signal optimization reduce idling, ease congestion and lower urban carbon footprints.

Tipping Point Atlas is a cooperative board game for 2–6 players who each govern a unique region with “Carbon Stock,” “Temperature” and “Ecosystem Health” tracks. Every turn you draw a Climate Feedback card that stresses one or more tracks, then spend limited Action cubes on six mitigation paths—Clean Energy, Reforestation, Ocean Health, Sustainable Agriculture, Community Resilience and Tech R&D. If any regional track crosses its Crisis line you must resolve a Tipping card (permafrost thaw, ocean current shift, mass die-off) that imposes new global stresses. Players may share cubes to support hard-hit regions or invest in Global Treaties that cap stress spikes. After twelve rounds, if no region has permanently tipped, the players win—learning how interconnected systems, resource trade-offs and collective action are vital to sustainable living.

Watt Watchers is a 2–5-player cooperative deduction board game in which players hunt “Energy Vampires” (hidden phantom‐load appliances) in a model home. At setup you secretly place Vampire tokens behind room tiles (Kitchen, Living Room, Bedroom, Garage). Each turn you spend limited Diagnostic tokens to draw Smart-Meter clues (cards indicating high, medium or low standby drain per room) or peek under a single tile. Once you deduce a room’s vampire, play an Action card (“Unplug Device,” “Install Smart Strip,” “Seal Standby Drain”) to remove it and reclaim energy on the Home Energy track. Failing to clear all vampires before the Energy Budget depletes causes a blackout and a loss. Cleared vampires earn Efficiency Points to buy permanent Upgrades (LED bulbs, programmable thermostat, smart plugs) that expand your budget in advanced scenarios. By investigating phantom loads, prioritizing interventions and investing in real solutions, Watt Watchers teaches how everyday devices stealthily waste energy and how targeted fixes drive sustainable living.

EcoCart Caper is a semi-cooperative push-your-luck board game for 2–6 players where you race through a supermarket filling a shared cart while managing weight, budget and carbon footprint. Each turn you draw an Item card (seasonal produce, plant-based proteins, imported goods, processed foods) and choose to add it to the cart—earning Nutrient points toward a communal Weekly Meal Plan—or pass to trigger Checkout. Every item adds weight (risking a spill if capacity is exceeded) and footprint (tracked on a carbon meter); three spills or an overfilled meter costs the group the game. At any time a player may “bank” cart contents into their personal pantry grid, reset the cart and unlock Bulk-Buy discounts that permanently reduce future footprints. After five shopping rounds, the group wins by meeting nutrient quotas, filling pantry objectives and staying under the carbon threshold—teaching how food choices, portion planning and seasonality trade-offs drive sustainable living.

Greenfluence is a semi‐cooperative card‐and‐token game for 3–6 players who play eco-influencers competing and collaborating to raise real-world sustainability awareness before their followers tune out. Each turn players draft Content cards (Recycling Reel, Plant-Based Recipe, Repair Tutorial) tagged with Reach, Resource Cost and Trust values, then spend Follower tokens to “post” them on a shared Feed board. Posts award Awareness Points, but overusing high-impact actions without genuine backing lowers the Trust Meter. Algorithm cards (Viral Boom, Platform Policy, Scandal) at the end of each round reshuffle the Feed, boosting some posts or burying others and shifting global Engagement and Trust meters. Players can pool Influence tokens to launch Community Challenges (Neighborhood Cleanup, Seed-bomb Drop) that permanently raise baseline awareness. The group wins if Awareness hits the target before Trust crashes; the top contributor claims the “Greenfluence” crown—having learned the balance between impactful messaging, authenticity and community action in sustainable living.

Green Mine is a semi-cooperative push-your-luck board game for 2–6 players who race to extract valuable minerals from an endangered region while balancing environmental harm and restoration. Each turn:

• Mine Phase: roll three colored dice to collect resource cubes (coal, metal, water); rerolls let you push for more but generate “Damage” tokens on habitat sites equal to dice you set aside.  
• Impact Phase: assign Damage tokens to three regional tiles (forest, wetland, grassland). When a tile reaches its collapse limit, it triggers an “Eco-crisis” that steals resources and costs points.  
• Remediation Phase: spend resource cubes to fund restoration actions (reforestation, wetland rebuild, water filtration) that remove Damage and earn Sustainability points.

After seven rounds, players total Victory points from mined resources minus Eco-crisis penalties plus Sustainability points. If no tile has collapsed, everyone earns a “Green Concession” bonus; the highest scorer wins. By weighing short-term gains against long-term repair costs, Green Mine teaches resource trade-offs, ecosystem fragility and the value of restoration in sustainable living.

“Trash to Treasure” is a semi-cooperative dexterity-and-creativity game for 2–6 players who reimagine household waste as functional sculptures. Over five timed rounds, each player draws 3–5 shaped “waste” blocks (bottles, caps, cartons) and a Challenge card (e.g. “Solar Lamp,” “Vertical Planter,” “Water Filter”). In 3 minutes they stack and attach blocks into a free-standing prototype. Creations are scored by the group for Functionality, Material Efficiency and Aesthetic Appeal, earning Sustainability Points. Unused blocks feed a communal Scrap Pile that unlocks “Community Builds” (e.g. public benches, garden modules) when thresholds are met, rewarding all players. After five rounds the highest scorer wins, and if the group completes at least three Community Builds they unlock a real-world upcycling kit. By forcing players to creatively repurpose waste under time and design constraints, Trash to Treasure teaches resourcefulness, circular-economy thinking and the environmental value of seeing landfill as raw material.

Terrarium Tinkerers is a cooperative board-and-terrarium game for 1–4 players who each maintain a mini closed-system terrarium while managing shared climate conditions. Each round you draw a Climate card (rainfall, sun cycle, temperature swing) then allocate water, light tokens or plant/soil cards to your terrarium board, adjusting its humidity, oxygen and nutrient meters. Players may trade resources or microbe cards to rescue struggling terrariums, and play Event cards (drought, pest outbreak) that test collective resilience. If all terrariums remain within balance thresholds until the global Biosphere Stability track fills, everyone wins—having learned closed-loop resource cycles, interdependence and proactive ecosystem care.

“Rooftop Revolution” is a cooperative tile‐placement game for 2–5 players transforming a dull city block into a net‐positive neighborhood. A modular board shows flat‐roof grids; on each turn players spend Worker tokens to place one Project tile—green roof, solar panel, rainwater tank, pollinator habitat or rooftop farm—paying its build cost and earning Resource tokens (energy, water, food, biodiversity). Adjacency grants synergy: rain catchers feed farms, pollinator tiles boost yields. Draw a Weather card (storm, drought, heatwave, sun) to test your setup; damaged or under‐buffered tiles lose output, while well‐linked networks resist shocks. Over six Seasonal cycles you must generate more resources than the community consumes on a shared tracker to win. By balancing trade‐offs, interconnections and weather risks, players learn how local projects compound into resilient, sustainable living.

“Aquaponic Architects” is a cooperative board-and-tile game for 2–4 players who build and manage a closed-loop aquaponic greenhouse. A modular greenhouse board has slots for Fish Tanks, Plant Beds, Biofilters and Water Pumps. Each turn players spend limited Water, Energy and Nutrient tokens to place or upgrade a module, then draw an Event card (disease outbreak, pump failure, drought) that tests water quality, fish health and plant growth metrics. Balanced systems earn Yield points; imbalances generate Stress cubes that must be removed by realigning modules or spending extra resources. After six growth cycles, if the collective Yield meets the greenhouse’s food-and-fish targets without any metric collapsing, players win—learning firsthand how nutrient cycling, water conservation and infrastructure choices interconnect in sustainable living.

Terra Firma is a cooperative board game for 2–5 players who take on the roles of planetary engineers tasked with terraforming a barren world into a living, sustainable ecosystem. The central board shows four interlinked sectors—Atmosphere, Hydrosphere, Lithosphere and Biosphere—each with a stability track. Each round:
1. Players draft Technology cards (e.g. Solar Mirrors, Desalination Towers, Mycorrhizal Networks, Algal Blooms) into their hand.
2. Allocate limited Engineer tokens to play cards, boosting one or more sector tracks at the cost of Resource tokens (Energy, Water, Minerals, Life).
3. Draw a Planet Event card (solar flare, dust storm, seismic shift, invasive microbe) that applies stress counters to sectors; players may spend buffered stability or emergency modules to avert collapse.

Completing full cycles of card play advances the Terraform Progress marker. If at any time a sector’s stability hits zero, the world suffers a setback and the Terraform marker retreats; if all four sectors stay above their danger thresholds until the Terraform marker reaches the finish, players win, having learned how integrated, balanced interventions and resource trade-offs are essential to sustainable living on any planet.

EcoStrata is a cooperative layered-tile game for 2–5 players who restore a degraded landscape across three interlocking ecosystem “strata”: Soil, Water and Canopy. Each turn players play Action cards (e.g. “Build Rain Garden,” “Inoculate with Mycorrhizae,” “Plant Native Trees”) to earn translucent tiles they place on a three-level board. Tile overlaps trigger synergy bonuses or conflicts (compaction under canopy, runoff over bare soil). After each “Season,” an Event card (drought, flash flood, pest outbreak) tests each layer’s Health track. If all three tracks meet their targets before the Event deck is exhausted, players win—learning how vertical interactions, timing and trade-offs sustain healthy ecosystems and resilient communities.

Green Pledge League is a hybrid board-and-app game for 2–6 players who commit to real-world green habits and see their impact unfold on a shared town board. Setup: lay out a modular town map with upgrade slots (solar panels, community garden, repair café, bike-share hub). Each week players draw two Challenge cards (e.g. “Meat-free day,” “Zero-waste shop,” “Bike commute”), secretly pick one to pledge, then log completion via the companion app (photo proof or simple yes/no). Successful pledges earn Community Points you spend to install upgrades on the board, unlocking lasting “buffs” that reduce future pledge difficulty; failures draw Setback cards that place Footprint markers on the town. After six weeks, if all upgrade slots are filled and total Footprint markers remain below the loss threshold, the group wins—having experienced firsthand how consistent daily choices compound into a resilient, sustainable community.

“Patchwork Planet” is a cooperative tile-placement game for 1–4 players who each build a 5×5 “sustainability quilt” of Fabric tiles representing green actions—Reforestation, Solar Canopy, Rain Garden, Repair Hub, Community Kitchen. On your turn you draft two tiles (each with thread-costs and resource-savings icons), pay with limited Thread tokens, and stitch your patch into your quilt grid, scoring adjacency bonuses when outputs (energy, water, waste reduction, social) line up. Every third round you reveal a Crisis card (storm surge, heat wave, supply chain shock) that removes or flips random tiles unless buffered by prior investments. After 12 rounds you total each quilt’s Resource Savings minus Thread spent; if the group’s collective Savings meets the Sustainability Threshold, everyone wins; the highest personal score earns “Master Quilter.” By fitting patches under resource limits and buffering crises, players learn trade-offs, adjacency synergies and the cumulative impact of everyday sustainable choices.

EcoMosaic is a cooperative jigsaw-style board game for 1–6 players who together assemble a 6×8 map by fitting irregular “land-use” puzzle pieces—Forest, Farmland, Wetland, Urban, Solar Farm and Community Garden. Each piece shows icons for water yield, carbon absorption, food or energy production and biodiversity. When edges match, adjacency bonuses apply (e.g. forests next to wetlands boost flood control; solar farms by roads ease transport). Each turn you place a piece and adjust four resource meters—Water, Food, Energy and Biodiversity—then draw an Event card (drought, heat wave, sprawl, rain boom) that may force swaps or impose deficits. If, when the mosaic is complete or the Event deck is exhausted, all meters meet their thresholds, the community thrives and you win. EcoMosaic teaches spatial planning, ecosystem interdependence and the trade-offs of sustainable land-use through hands-on, cooperative puzzle-building.

Sustainababble is a semi‐cooperative word‐building board game for 2–6 players who draft letter tiles (each printed with a real‐world carbon cost) to form “green” words on a shared grid. Each word earns Sustainability Points equal to its letter values but also adds Footprint tokens matching its total carbon cost. Placing words on Community Hub spaces doubles points or halves footprint. After each of eight rounds players draw a Crisis card (heatwave, flood, policy shake‐up) forcing the group to spend Footprint tokens or lose Infrastructure tokens. If by the end the shared Sustainability Meter (sum of all players’ SP minus spent Footprint) meets its threshold, all win; the highest‐scoring lexicographer claims the EcoWordsmith title. Sustainababble teaches that every choice—even a word—carries environmental cost, highlighting strategic planning, collaboration and trade‐offs in sustainable living.

“EcoData: Carbon Cloud Managers” is a cooperative board game for 2–5 players who run a global cloud network. Each round:  
1. Draw a Workload card (video stream, AI task, backup) with CPU, storage and latency demands.  
2. Allocate Workload tokens to Data Center tiles—each tile shows its energy mix (renewables vs. grid), PUE (power usage efficiency) and water-cooling rating—and pay energy and water tokens accordingly.  
3. Spend Development points to upgrade servers (low-PUE modules, liquid-cooling rigs, e-waste recycling), buy green energy credits or build on-site renewables.  
4. Resolve a Data Surge event (heatwave, network spike, component recall) that forces extra energy draw or hardware breakdowns.  

Each Data Center tracks a Carbon meter and an E-Waste meter; if either exceeds its safe threshold, all players suffer latency penalties (slower resource allocation). After 10 rounds, if total Carbon footprint and E-Waste remain under global targets and all Workloads met their SLAs, the network thrives and players win—revealing how digital services carry hidden environmental costs and teaching energy sourcing, efficiency upgrades and hardware lifecycles as keys to sustainable living.

“Sustainable Sushi Showdown” is a competitive card‐drafting game for 2–4 players who each run a sushi stall aiming to satisfy customer orders while protecting the ocean. Each round:
1. Reveal 2–4 Order cards specifying rolls (e.g. salmon avocado, eel cucumber) with points for Taste and Sustainability.  
2. Draft Ingredient cards—Fish (tuna, salmon, octopus), Rice, Seaweed, Veggies—each bearing Carbon, Water and Biodiversity footprints and seasonal availability.  
3. Pay Resource tokens or spend Research points to upgrade to sustainable sourcing (aquaculture, regenerative rice paddies, seaweed farms).  
4. Assemble Roll sets to fulfill Orders: you score Taste points minus footprint penalties; unfilled Orders cost global Sustainability points.  
5. Draw an Event (red tide, shipping delay, subsidy) that may make certain ingredients scarce or grant rebates.

After five rounds the player with the highest net Taste + Upgrade points wins, but if the shared Sustainability Meter never falls below the threshold, all win a “Community Resilience” bonus—teaching how menu choices, seasonality and investment in sustainable supply chains balance enjoyment with environmental stewardship.

Paths to Tomorrow is a branching‐story card game for 1–4 players. Over 12 “days” you draw a Story card outlining a real-life scenario (commute, meal, community meeting) and choose between two Actions, each showing its carbon, water and social-cohesion impacts. Resolve by drawing a Consequence card—some permanently reshape the deck or trigger Events (drought, power outage, subsidy) you must mitigate. Fact cards inserted at key junctures offer bite-size lessons and bonus sustainable actions you can take for extra meter boosts. Track three shared meters—Carbon, Water and Community Cohesion—and if all stay above critical levels at day 12, you unlock an epilogue showing your town’s transformation and win. By weaving narrative choices with evolving deck dynamics and meter management, Paths to Tomorrow teaches how daily decisions and collaborative solutions compound into lasting sustainable living.

C:N Quest is a cooperative card-and-tile game for 2–5 players who act as compost engineers racing to turn household waste into mature, pathogen-free compost before winter arrives. Each turn:
• Draft Waste cards (vegetable scraps, paper, coffee grounds), each showing C and N values.  
• Place them into your shared Compost Pile and manage Moisture tokens and Aeration tiles to maintain an optimal C:N ratio (~30:1).  
• Draw Event cards (rainstorm, heatwave, pest outbreak) that force you to add Water tokens, insert Aeration sticks or remove Infestation markers.  
If at any point the pile’s temperature (tracked on a dial) falls outside 50–70 °C or pests overwhelm your defenses, you suffer setbacks. Over ten rounds, if you achieve three full “Mature Compost” tiles without collapse, you win—learning real-world compost science, waste sorting and ecosystem balancing in sustainable living.

Sunracers is a semi-competitive tabletop race for 2–4 players who each build and tune a miniature solar-powered car from modular chassis, panel, battery and aerodynamic shell pieces. Each round (“heat”):
• Spend limited Eco-Points to attach or upgrade solar panels, storage cells and drag-reduction parts.
• Place your car under a movable lamp (“sun”) on a modular track and set panel angles.
• Draw a Weather card (sunny, cloudy, windy) that modifies lamp intensity or activates a wind-fan, then release your car and measure its glide distance.
• Score Eco-Points for distance and energy efficiency (distance ÷ simulated wattage).
Between heats, invest Eco-Points in personal upgrades or shared infrastructure (solar tracker mounts, wind tunnels) that boost all cars. After six heats, the highest combined personal and community Eco-Points wins. Sunracers teaches solar capture, storage trade-offs and aerodynamic design for sustainable transportation.

“Homestead Harmony” is a cooperative worker‐placement board game for 2–5 players who jointly manage a rural homestead to achieve energy, food and ecosystem balance. Each “day” you assign meeples to tasks—tilling permaculture beds, feeding livestock, harvesting rainwater, maintaining solar panels or building composters—earning or spending four Resource tokens (Food, Biofuel, Soil Fertility, Electricity). At day’s end draw a Weather or Market Event (drought, price spike, storm) that tests your infrastructure and forces trade-offs. Successful tasks upgrade modular tiles (greenhouse, biogas digester, windmill, pond) that buffer future crises and unlock advanced actions. After twelve days, if your collective Crop Yield, Animal Welfare, Soil Health and Energy Autonomy all meet their thresholds, you win—learning how diversified cycles, shared labor and resilient systems underpin sustainable living.

Droplet Dash is a cooperative board game for 2–6 players who each pilot a water droplet through the full water cycle—Ocean, Evaporation, Cloud, Precipitation, River and Groundwater. On your turn you roll to advance, then draw a Pollution card (agricultural runoff, plastic debris, industrial discharge) that adds Contamination tokens to your droplet. To purify, players spend Action cards—Wetlands Filter, Green Roof, Riparian Buffer, Wastewater Treatment—or contribute shared Resource cubes to Community Projects (River Cleanup, Riparian Restoration) to remove tokens. Special “Flash Flood” or “Drought” events force regional checks: if pollution exceeds local thresholds you lose Action cards. After each droplet completes three full cycles, you tally remaining Contamination tokens; if the group’s total purity score meets the target you win—having learned how green infrastructure, land-use choices and collective investment maintain clean water and sustainable living.

Savannah Stewards is a cooperative board game for 1–4 players who play wildlife rangers managing an African reserve’s ecology, economy and community. On a modular savannah board divided into grassland, waterhole and woodland zones, each round you assign Ranger tokens to:
• Guided Eco-Tours (earn Revenue but add Stress to wildlife)  
• Anti-Poaching Patrols (remove Poacher tokens)  
• Habitat Restoration (plant trees, dig water pans)  
• Community Outreach (trade goods for local support)  
Revenue builds infrastructure tiles (solar wells, wildlife corridors, ranger posts) that buffer Stress and boost animal populations. After each round draw an Event card (drought, disease, protest, poacher surge) that tests zone Stability tracks. If wildlife populations and community Trust remain above thresholds after eight seasons, all win—learning how balancing tourism, conservation, ecosystem restoration and local engagement drives truly sustainable living.

EcoOffice is a cooperative board game for 2–6 players who manage a corporate office’s sustainability over a 12-month cycle. Each month, players assign Staff meeples to departments—Energy, Waste, Water, Commuting or Procurement—to run projects (e.g. energy audits, recycling stations, car-pool programs) that generate Resource Savings tokens and Sustainability Points. A Monthly Event card (audit, equipment failure, policy shift) tests each department’s targets; failures add Carbon Footprint tokens. Players spend Savings tokens to unlock Office Upgrades—solar panels, greywater loops, on-site composting—that buff future actions. If by month 12 the office’s total Carbon Footprint stays below the corporate threshold and Sustainability Points reach the goal, all win—learning how cross-department coordination, project prioritization and strategic investments drive sustainable operations in a real-world workplace.

Rescue Kitchen is a cooperative set-collection board game for 2–5 players as urban food-rescue volunteers racing spoilage. Over four “Shifts” you assign Volunteer meeples to Harvest sites (farms, grocers, restaurants) to collect Surplus Ingredient cards—each source shows pickup windows and spoilage risk. You spend limited Transport tokens to move between sites; late pickups or overfilled routes generate Waste markers. Collected ingredients slot into shared Recipe boards requiring fruit, veg, grains or proteins to earn Nutrition points. After each Shift an Event card (traffic jam, cooling failure, donation surge) triggers spoilage checks or bonus pickups. Between Shifts spend Nutrition points on Storage Upgrades (refrigerated van, coordination app) that lower future spoilage. At game’s end, if your group’s total Nutrition meets community demand while Waste stays below the threshold, you win—learning how timely coordination, improved logistics and resource sharing reduce food waste and promote sustainable living.

Solar Sailors: The Renewable Regatta is a cooperative/competitive engineering-dexterity game for 2–6 players who each build and race a small solar-powered model boat. At setup you draft a limited supply of Hull, Solar-Panel and Battery modules. Each “Leg” you adjust panel angle, swap batteries or add hull weight before launching on a water track. Draw a Weather card (sunny, cloudy, choppy) to modify power output or steering stability. Boats that reach the finish earn Distance points; unused battery charge and unspent modules earn Sustainability points. Over three Legs the highest combined score wins. Through real-time construction, weather-driven power management and trade-offs between speed and efficiency, Solar Sailors teaches how panel placement, storage capacity and environmental variability shape sustainable renewable-energy design.

EcoFunders is a cooperative card-and-token game for 2–5 players acting as impact investors in a developing region. Each round players draw Microloan cards—sustainable ventures like solar kiosks, rainwater harvesters or compost cooperatives—each showing capital cost, risk level and resource‐savings metrics (energy, water, waste). Players pool or split their Capital tokens to fund loans, then draw Repayment cards influenced by economic and environmental Event cards (drought, subsidy, market swing). Successful loans return capital plus interest and award Sustainability Points; defaults cost capital and add Stress tokens. Players may spend points to buy Guarantee tokens insuring high-risk loans. After twelve rounds, if total Sustainability Points meet the global Impact Target and the group’s capital reserves remain solvent, all win—learning how risk assessment, collaborative funding and long-term investment drive community-level sustainable living.

EcoSync City is a cooperative hybrid board-and-app game for 2–5 players who link their real-world resource meters (or manually log daily energy, water and waste figures) into the EcoSync companion app. The board depicts a fledgling city divided into four zones (Energy, Water, Waste and Mobility), each with upgrade tracks for green infrastructure: solar arrays, rain gardens, compost hubs and bike-share docks. Each morning, real or logged usage is converted into Resource Points that players allocate to build or buffer zones before a weekly Crisis card (heatwave, drought, waste surge or traffic crush) strikes. Over four “seasons” players must keep every zone’s Stress meter below critical by balancing habit changes (in-game Habit cards recommending real-life actions), infrastructure investments and Crisis responses. If the city’s overarching Sustainability meter reaches 100% by game’s end, everyone wins, having learned how concrete daily choices compound into resilient, sustainable communities.

“EcoCruise Command” is a cooperative board game for 2–5 players who run a week-long eco-cruise. Each day you allocate limited Crew Action tokens across four departments—Energy (solar sails, kinetic recovery), Water (desalination, greywater loops), Waste (composting, bioplastic recycling) and Guest Experience (plant-based menus, eco-tours). Draw Passenger cards with comfort and thrill demands to satisfy with your systems, then resolve an Event card (storm swell, port emissions audit, algal bloom) that tests your resource buffers: insufficient storage or treatment raises your Carbon, Water or Waste footprints and dents Reputation. At the end of seven days, if all three footprints stay below their thresholds and Reputation remains high, you win—having learned the real-world trade-offs of guest satisfaction, system buffering and sustainable operations at sea.

“Plastic Pirates” is a semi-cooperative board-and-token game for 2–6 players who sail a modular ocean board divided into cleanup zones. Each turn you navigate your ship, gather differently colored Plastic tokens (PET bottles, film wrap, microplastics) into your hold, then return to port to sort, recycle or upcycle them for Resource points. Unprocessed or mis‐sorted tokens generate Pollution markers that drift into wildlife zones. Periodic “Current Surge” events reshuffle plastics between zones or introduce microplastic fallout that must be filtered. Between voyages you spend Resources on vessel upgrades (solar-driven shredder, filtering nets) and community campaigns (beach art, policy lobby) that permanently reduce spawn rates or boost processing efficiency. The players win by reducing total Plastic volumes in all zones below the cleanup target before Pollution markers overwhelm any wildlife area. By tracking token types, balancing collection versus processing, investing in tech and advocacy, Plastic Pirates teaches the lifecycle of plastics, the trade-offs of different recycling methods and the integrated strategies needed for real-world sustainable living.

EcoChess is a two‐player strategic board game on an 8×8 grid where each chess‐style piece (Pawn, Knight, Bishop, etc.) carries a carbon footprint. Every move or capture adds your piece’s footprint to a shared Climate Meter; if it crosses thresholds, “Heatwave” events restrict piece mobility. Instead of moving, you may spend a turn and Energy Tokens to “Green Upgrade” a piece, halving its future footprint. Victory comes by checkmating your opponent’s King before the Climate Meter triggers three global crises—or by checkmating with the Meter still below the loss threshold. EcoChess teaches players to balance tactical goals with the environmental costs of each action.

“Salvage Squad” is a cooperative board game for 2–5 players who play community salvage operators transforming derelict buildings into sustainable assets. A modular neighborhood board features old structures marked with Salvage icons (wood, metal, concrete, fixtures) and Hazard zones. Each turn players assign Crew tokens to:

• Deconstruct – clear debris and reveal Salvage resources  
• Sort – allocate materials into the community depot  
• Remediate – spend resources to neutralize Hazards (asbestos, rot, weather damage)  
• Build – use salvaged materials to install Community Tiles (solar pavilion, rain garden, bike repair shop)  

Each building yields different material mixes and may trigger Hazard cards that block actions or consume protective gear. Completed Community Tiles lower the shared Footprint meter and unlock bonus effects (e.g. “Stormwater Capture” buffers next rain event). Event cards (grant funding, policy changes, vandalism) alter resource availability or introduce new challenges. After eight rounds, if the Footprint meter reaches the sustainability threshold and all community needs are met, players win—learning circular building practices, trade-offs in deconstruction methods, hazard management and how salvaging materials fosters resilient, sustainable living.

Heirloom Harvest – a 2–4-player cooperative board game about seed saving and climate-resilient farming. Each round, players assign Farmers to “Plant,” “Harvest,” “Research” heirloom varieties or “Trade” seeds with neighbors. Harvests generate Food and Diversity points, but Event cards (frost, drought, pest outbreak, market crash) test your resilience: lacking sufficient genetic Diversity forces you to discard crops. Spent points fund Community Upgrades—rainwater cisterns, pollinator habitats, low-till tools—that permanently buffer future crises. After six Seasons, if the group’s total Food meets village demand and Diversity stays above the collapse threshold, everyone wins—learning how crop variety, seed sharing and regenerative practices drive sustainable living.
